tagline.text: A 4.2 km underground-river cave hidden in the mountains of Nueva Vizcaya

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,000 (per person; guide, entrance, homestay and local transport, excluding round-trip transport from Manila)

children.text: Capisaan Cave is a limestone cave system about 4.2 km long in a mountain village of Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya, and is said to be the fifth-longest cave in the Philippines. Wearing a helmet and life vest, you wade across an underground river and pass through chambers of cave formations on an adventure route that takes anywhere from half a day to a full day with a guide.

Capisaan Cave lies in the mountainous municipality of Kasibu in Nueva Vizcaya province, in the Cagayan Valley region of northern Luzon, in the barangay of Capisaan. Rather than a single cave, it is a system of several caves, such as Lion Cave and Alayan Cave, that were found to connect, which is why it is also called the Alayan–Lion Cave. Its total length is said to be about
4.2 km

, and it is described as the fifth-longest cave system in the Philippines. Sources list eight or nine entrances, and the Lion, Alayan and Sabrina entrances are the ones mainly used. Kasibu is a mountain municipality about
300 km
from Manila and about
46 km
from the provincial capital, Bayombong.

The appeal of this cave is that it is not a cave dressed up for tourists. At the entrance you attend an orientation and receive a helmet, headlamp and life vest, then follow your guide into the dark. Inside are large chambers and an underground river, followed by limestone features such as stalactites, stalagmites, soda straws (thin hollow stalactites) and helictites (twisting crystal growths). Bats roost in several places, and you may also see fish and crabs that have washed in from nearby tributaries. The water is very cold, and some sections have you hold a rope to cross deep water or climb a steep slope on a rope, so this is a far more physical experience than a walk-through cave.

The history is interesting too. The area was originally rainforest, and people are said to have begun settling here around 1960. Residents hunted bats and gathered edible bird's nests at the cave entrances. Cave trekking tours began in the 1990s; guides first used kerosene lamps, but these were banned because the fumes harmed the cave. Exploration by caving clubs showed that Lion Cave and Alayan Cave are connected, which made the long cave system known, and the First National Caving Congress held in Nueva Vizcaya in 2001 spread its name widely. The name "Capisaan Cave" then replaced the earlier names.

Even today the cave is an adventure destination that local government is actively promoting. According to a Nueva Vizcaya provincial government report, on June 10–11, 2026 the provincial tourism and culture office and the Kasibu municipal tourism office held the "Capisaan C3 (Caving, Camping and Coffee) Experience," in which more than 100 visitors split into ten groups and traveled the cave's halfway route. A cave management plan was also handed over at that event. This guide is for travelers who want to visit the cave on a 2-day, 1-night trip from Manila, and it covers how to get there, routes, what to bring and what to watch out for. Fees and operating arrangements change often, so be sure to confirm with the Capisaan information center before you go.
This route crosses the whole cave system from the Lion entrance to the Alayan entrance (or the reverse) and usually takes
5–6 hours
. The time depends on your pace and the water level, and it is the main route most travelers choose.

blocks.title: Halfway-start short route from Sang-at Salug

children.text: Starting at Sang-at Salug (the cave's midpoint) and exiting toward Lion or Alayan takes about
2–3 hours
. It suits beginners who are worried about stamina or short on time, and this halfway route was also used at the June 2026 event.

An underground river flows through the cave, and there are sections where you hold a rope to cross deep water or cross a stream by swimming or a rope tightrope. Life vests are issued as required equipment, and the water is very cold. Go expecting to get wet.

There are varied formations, including large chambers, stalactites, stalagmites, soda straws and helictites, and bat colonies in several places. Touching crystals damages them, so touch only what your guide points out, and pass the bats quietly so you do not disturb them.

You face a series of challenges: a stretch where water rains from the ceiling, tight gaps where you must stoop and crawl, and a steep slope climbed with a rope. Your guide shows you where to place your hands and feet, so just follow slowly.

Registration and guide assignment are handled at the Capisaan information center in the village. Accredited homestays near the cave provide lodging and meals, so staying a night here and spending the evening in the mountain village makes for a natural itinerary.

The 2026 C3 event also featured a coffee farm tour, a hike on the Capisaan eco-trail and a visit to a weaving community. They are worth considering when planning activities beyond the cave, but ask at the information center whether they operate regularly now.

Many trip reports combine nearby waterfalls such as Imugan Falls and Lintungan Falls with the cave on a 2-day, 1-night plan. A typical pattern is to leave Manila on an overnight trip, visit a waterfall at dawn, go caving in the afternoon, and finish the next day with another waterfall and a church visit.

items.title: 2-day, 1-night route
items.subtitle: Cave exploration and a mountain homestay

children.text: Take an overnight bus from Manila toward the Cagayan Valley and get off at Solano in Nueva Vizcaya. Arrive early, have breakfast and look for a jeepney to Kasibu.
Take a jeepney from Solano or Bambang toward Kasibu. Much of the road is a dirt road cut into mountainsides, so allow plenty of time.
Arrive at the Capisaan information center, register, and receive your guide and equipment (helmet, headlamp and life vest). Have lunch at your homestay.
Attend the orientation and enter the cave. The halfway route takes about 2–3 hours and the long route 5–6 hours, so choose a route that lets you exit before sunset.
Shower and have dinner at the homestay. Once the sun sets, the mountain village quickly goes quiet.
After breakfast the next day, leave the homestay and visit a nearby waterfall or coffee farm, then take a jeepney out to Solano or Bambang in the afternoon and board a bus to Manila.
The last jeepney out toward Solano leaves early, so ask the information center or your homestay host in advance when you need to head down.

items.title: Self-drive or rental car route
items.subtitle: A two-day plan combining waterfalls and the cave

children.text: Leave Manila and enter the mountain roads of Nueva Vizcaya. Public transport is sparse, so having a vehicle makes the route much easier.
Take an early walk at Imugan Falls, then continue to central Kasibu for check-in and lunch.
Explore Capisaan Cave on either the halfway route or the long route.
The next day, visit a nearby waterfall such as Lintungan Falls, stop at Bayombong Cathedral, and return to Manila.
Mountain roads are known for frequent landslides and traffic delays, so leave extra time for the return trip.

From Manila (northern terminals such as Cubao or Genesis), take a bus toward the Cagayan Valley (Santiago, Cauayan, Tuguegarao and so on) and get off at Solano in Nueva Vizcaya. One trip report says the ride from Manila to the Solano area took about
6 hours
(based on the Santa Fe route; it varies with traffic).
At Solano, transfer to a jeepney bound for Kasibu. The distance from Solano to Kasibu is about
51 km
, and one source says the jeepney ride took
3–4 hours
It is also known that you can get off a Santa Fe-bound bus and continue to Kasibu by jeepney or tricycle.
Bus schedules and last jeepney times change often. Check with the terminal and the information center before you leave.
Jeepneys leave Bambang toward Capisaan. One trip report says the last departure is around 12–1 PM, the ride takes at least about
2 hours 30 minutes
and the fare is about
. Kasibu is about
31 km
from Bambang.
Because public transport is limited, many travelers use a rental car or van arranged by someone who knows the area.
You can also fly from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to a northern Luzon airport such as Tuguegarao and continue south overland. Check the airline's announcements for routes and times.
By car from Manila the distance is about
300 km
, and the mountain sections may take longer than a map app estimates.
In Capisaan village, the information center, homestays and cave entrance are close together, so you mostly get around on foot.
Trip reports say there is weak mobile signal and no ATM, so bring plenty of cash.
Kasibu is a high mountain area, so average temperatures are on the cool side. According to Wikipedia, monthly mean temperatures range from about

, annual rainfall is about 2,000 mm, and June to October is the wettest period. Cave exploration is affected by the level of the underground river, so in rainy months routes may be limited or the trip may have to be postponed.

In general, the drier winter and spring months (November–May) are good for exploring. However, the water inside the cave is cold in every season, so in the cool months of December–February wet clothes can feel colder. A trip report advises adjusting plans if heavy rain continues, so ask the information center about the weather and water level first.

Accredited homestays operate in the village, including near the Capisaan information center. One trip report says a homestay across from the information center also provided meals. There are no large hotels, and bedding and showers are simple, so bring a jacket or a thin blanket for the chilly nights. Some sources say reservations are not required, but on peak seasons and weekends it is safer to contact the Capisaan Cave Tour Guides Association first.

Meals are mostly taken at your homestay, and the village has almost no large restaurants. The area is also known for coffee and citrus fruit, so you can try local coffee. Prepare snacks and water to take into the cave.

Before you leave, check fees, operations and weather with the Capisaan information center or the Capisaan Cave Tour Guides Association on Facebook. The information center is said to be open daily from 08:00 to 17:00 all year.

Wear light long sleeves and long pants (leggings or trekking pants), a quick-dry shirt or rash guard, and trekking sandals or aqua shoes. Slippers are not allowed, and aqua shoes can reportedly be rented at the registration area.
Put your phone and wallet in a waterproof dry bag, and bring a camera or phone that works well in low light. A spare headlamp can be rented.
The water in the cave is cold, so pack dry clothes to change into, a towel and plastic bags. Mountain nights are cool, so bring a jacket as well.
Tipping your guide is a customary practice. Prepare a modest amount in cash to show your thanks.
Choose a route that fits your stamina. The halfway route (2–3 hours) and long route (5–6 hours) differ greatly in difficulty and time, so start around 1 PM so you can exit before dark.
Bring plenty of cash. Trip reports say the village has no ATM and weak mobile signal.
Do not touch the cave formations or crystals, and do not leave trash. Do not shine a flash or light directly on the bats.
Children aged 10 and under are reportedly not allowed, and the cave involves crossing deep water and rope sections, so do not push yourself if you are a weak swimmer or strongly claustrophobic.
When it rains, water levels inside the cave can rise and plans can change. Guidance says to postpone if heavy rain continues, so follow your guide's judgment.
Mountain roads are known for frequent landslides and traffic delays, so leave extra time in your return schedule. Do not miss the last bus to Manila.

In 2017, clashes between the army and armed groups in the Kasibu uplands led the governor to advise tourists to hold off on visiting. The site now runs well enough to host a local government event in 2026, but check the latest announcements from the provincial and municipal tourism offices before you go.
Fees and rules differ by source (a 2022 trip report lists a ₱2,000 package, another reports ₱250 per person, and so on). Confirm exact amounts at the local information center and keep your receipt.
Prepare insurance and a personal first-aid kit in case of injury. A large hospital is far from the village and weak signal makes communication difficult.
Do not separate from your group to take photos. Always move together with your guide.
A waterfall in Imugan village in Nueva Vizcaya, often combined with the cave in a one-day plan in trip reports. Confirm the road and access details locally.
Waterfalls known in the Nueva Vizcaya area include Lintungan, Alimadin, Mapalyao and Diffuncian. Adding one or two before or after your cave trip works well.
A church in the provincial capital, Bayombong, often included on the way back to Manila. It is about
46 km
from Kasibu.
These were the activities featured at the 2026 C3 event. Ask at the information center whether you can add a day to see them.
